title: Ashtpadi 13, salok: the holy

cards: Who's the best person you actually know? Not the most well-known, not the most impressive. The best.
Maybe a neighbor who shovels the whole block's sidewalks and never mentions it. An aunt who remembers every birthday. A nurse who stayed after her shift.
Now the harder question: have you ever told them? Applause is easy to give a stranger on a stage. It's oddly hard to give the neighbor with the shovel.
The salok of the thirteenth ashtpadi starts right there: with the good ones, and what it means to stand near them.

teach.b: The salok's two lines pull in opposite directions. The first, in paraphrase: whoever takes shelter with the saints is carried across. The second: whoever slanders the saints, Nanak, is born again and again.
Today we stay with the first; tomorrow the ashtpadi turns to the second, and stays there a long time. First, the word.
Sant is usually translated saint, but careful: in the Guru Granth Sahib it isn't a rank anyone hands out.

teach.h: SANT: A LIFE SOAKED IN THE NAME.
teach.b: It describes a person whose life is soaked in remembering God: honest, humble, kind, steady. Sukhmani has described such people already, the holy company and the God-conscious one. They might run a shop.
Next, the verb: saran, shelter, refuge, the way you'd step under an awning when it rains. The salok isn't asking you to worship good people. It says nearness to them changes you.
Sikhs call it sangat, the company, and Sikh worship gathers around it: praying together, singing together, eating together in the langar.
Goodness, in this picture, is catching. Stand near it long enough and some of it rubs off, the way a cloth takes on the scent of the flowers it's wrapped around.
And the second line hangs over the first like a cloud: if nearness lifts you, contempt for the good drags you down. That's tomorrow.
Today: notice the good people, and honor them.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib reach the thirteenth ashtpadi's salok on the sant, and Sikh life places great weight on sangat, the company of the good, in shared prayer, singing and the langar.

o: a title given only after a person dies
a person whose life is soaked in God
a monk who has left family and work

games.q: the salok of the holy — tap the pairs.
p: a life soaked in remembering God

s: in Sukhmani, a sant is someone officially declared holy
a sant is anyone whose life is soaked in the Name; it could be your grandmother.
the salok of the thirteenth ashtpadi has two lines pulling opposite ways
shelter with the saints carries you across; slandering them sends you round again.
the salok asks people to worship good people
it speaks of shelter: nearness to the good changes you.

games.q: you know someone quietly, deeply good. by the salok, what's the gift in that?
o: you can ask them for favors.
standing near them, some of their goodness rubs off.
you can tell everyone you know them.
games.why: the salok speaks of saran, shelter: nearness to the holy carries you across. Sikhs call that company sangat.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose goodness is quiet, see their face, and remember one specific thing they did; a small one is best.
Hold it there and let yourself be grateful that people like this exist, picturing, if you like, telling them so in one plain sentence. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Sant, a holy person. Soaked in remembering God; shelter near such people, the salok says, carries you across.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sant, a holy person; in the Guru Granth Sahib, one whose life is soaked in the Name.

carryVoice: Your line: honor the good. Goodness is catching, like scent on a cloth. See you tomorrow.
